subtitle: A guide to the family of remote network monitoring specifications

tldr.problem: Network management systems need to monitor distributed networks in real time, detect faults quickly, and gather historical data for analysis. A monolithic single specification cannot address the diverse needs of layer 2 link monitoring, layer 3 routing, layer 4 transport performance, and application-level metrics.
tldr.mechanism: RMON is not a single specification but a framework of interconnected MIB modules. Each module focuses on a specific layer or function (Ethernet statistics, protocol analysis, host traffic, packet capture, alarms, and higher-layer extensions). Monitors gather data continuously, store it locally, and notify management stations of faults.
tldr.outcome: The framework accommodates offline operation (monitors work even when disconnected), proactive monitoring (continuous diagnostics), problem detection with thresholds, and value-added analysis. Multiple modules can work together in a single implementation.

today: RFC 3577 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted. It remains the definitive guide to the RMON family of specifications. RMON standards continue to evolve, and the document's framework approach allows new modules to be added without obsoleting the whole family.

sections.title: What Is Remote Monitoring (RMON)
sections.content:
Remote Monitoring (RMON) refers to network monitoring devices, or probes, that watch network traffic and report statistics to a management station. Originally, RMON probes were dedicated hardware devices that sat on a network segment and analyzed traffic. Over time, RMON capability moved into routers, switches, and software applications.

A key feature of RMON is offline operation: the probe continues to collect statistics, run diagnostics, and log alarms even when the management station is offline or unreachable. When communication is restored, the probe reports accumulated data and alerts. This is crucial for networks where the management station is connected over a slow or unreliable link.

Another key feature is proactive monitoring: the probe runs continuous diagnostics and stores historical data, making it possible to correlate fault events with historical trends and to perform root cause analysis after the fact.

In the beginning, most RMON probes captured packets promiscuously from a network segment. Modern RMON modules use diverse data sources: some still use packet capture, others query switch statistics, and others perform application-level analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: An RMON probe is like a dedicated watcher on the network. It watches all the time, remembers what happened, and sends alerts when something breaks. It can work even if the management system is not watching.

sections.title: The RMON Framework and Module Layers
sections.content:
The RMON Framework is not one specification but a collection of MIB modules, each defining managed objects for a specific monitoring function. These modules operate at different measurement layers (where they collect data) and aggregation layers (how they group the data).

RMON-1 (RFC 2819) focuses on layer 2 (link layer) and measures Ethernet statistics: packets, bytes, errors. It provides per-interface statistics, historical trends, host statistics, and conversation statistics between MAC address pairs. It also defines alarms (threshold monitoring) and packet capture.

RMON-2 (RFC 2021) extends RMON to layers 3 and above. It measures the same link-layer metrics but aggregates them by network address (IP), transport protocol, and application protocol. For example, it can report "how much HTTP traffic is there," not just "how much traffic on this Ethernet."

Token Ring Extensions (RFC 1513) add RMON monitoring for Token Ring media, a pre-Ethernet networking technology. They mirror RMON-1 concepts for Token Ring.

Additional modules extend RMON into specialized areas: SMON for switched networks, HCRMON for high-capacity interfaces, APM for application performance (layer 7), TPM for transport protocol metrics (layer 4), DSMON for Differentiated Services, SSPM for synthetic monitoring, and RAQMON for application quality-of-service.
sections.plainLanguage: RMON is like a toolbox. One tool watches Ethernet traffic, another watches protocols, another watches applications. Different tools work at different depths, and you can use them together.

sections.title: Core RMON-1 Functions
sections.content:
The main RMON-1 specification defines nine functional groups:

Statistics Group: Counts packets, bytes, and errors per Ethernet interface.

History Group: Records periodic snapshots of statistics over time, allowing trends to be seen.

Host Group: Discovers hosts on the network (by watching source and destination MAC addresses in good packets) and maintains traffic statistics per host.

Host Top-N Group: Generates ranked reports of hosts (e.g., top 10 bandwidth users) during a specified interval, with rate-based statistics.

Matrix Group: Tracks conversations between pairs of MAC addresses and counts packets and bytes in each direction.

Filter Group: Allows packets matching a filter expression to be identified and either counted or captured.

Packet Capture Group: Captures packet contents (after they match a filter) for later retrieval and analysis.

Alarm Group: Monitors any SNMP variable and compares it to high and low thresholds periodically. When a threshold is crossed, an event is generated. Hysteresis prevents flapping.

Event Group: Controls how events are logged and how management stations are notified (via SNMP traps or via syslog).
sections.plainLanguage: RMON-1 watches traffic on a link, finds the busiest hosts, tracks conversations, can catch traffic matching patterns, and sends alarms when numbers get too high or too low.

sections.title: RMON-2: Protocol and Application Analysis
sections.content:
RMON-2 extends the framework by adding protocol awareness and higher-layer aggregation. Key additions include:

Protocol Directory Group: Inventories the protocol types the probe can recognize (IPv4, TCP, HTTP, DNS, etc.) and allows management stations to add, remove, or configure which protocols to track.

Protocol Distribution Group: Counts packet and byte totals for each protocol seen on the interface. A management station can quickly determine bandwidth allocation by protocol.

Address Mapping Group: Lists MAC-to-IP address bindings discovered promiscuously and shows on which interface each binding was last seen.

Network Layer Host Group: Counts traffic sent from and to each IP address (replacing MAC-address-based host statistics with IP-based ones).

Network Layer Matrix Group: Counts traffic between IP address pairs, replacing the MAC-layer matrix.

Application Layer Host Group and Matrix: Similar to network-layer groups but aggregated by application (HTTP, SMTP, etc.).

These additions require the probe to parse packets deeply, recognizing protocols at multiple layers. This is more resource-intensive than layer 2 monitoring but provides much richer management visibility.
sections.plainLanguage: RMON-2 goes deeper into packets. Instead of just counting traffic, it recognizes protocols and applications, and can tell you how much email or web traffic there is.

sections.title: Specialized RMON Extensions
sections.content:
The RMON Framework has grown with specialized modules:

Switched Networks (SMON): Adds monitoring for switched Ethernet, addressing scenarios where traditional promiscuous packet capture is not possible on modern switched infrastructure.

High-Capacity Interfaces (HCRMON): Extends RMON-1 to gigabit-speed interfaces, where 32-bit counters overflow quickly. Uses 64-bit counters.

Application Performance Measurement (APM): Measures application-layer metrics like response time and transaction success rates, not just packet counts.

Transport Performance Metrics (TPM): Monitors transport-layer performance (TCP retransmissions, connection setup time, etc.).

Synthetic Monitoring (SSPM): Allows probes to generate synthetic test traffic (fake requests, pings, DNS lookups) and measure response performance from the network's perspective.

Differentiated Services (DSMON): Monitors performance of DiffServ traffic classes and ensures QoS policies are being honored.

Quality of Service (RAQMON): Measures real-time application quality (packet loss, delay, jitter) as experienced by application flows.

These modules can be layered: a single probe might implement RMON-1, RMON-2, and SMON together, or add APM and RAQMON for application insights.
sections.plainLanguage: As networks evolved, people added modules for switches, fast links, applications, quality, and synthetic testing. Each module measures something specific, and a probe can use many at once.
